problem: 'A passive sensor ... converts nothing' is wrong and contradicts Section 1 ('Every sensor is a transducer'). A passive sensor does convert the measurand — into a change of resistance, inductance or capacitance. What it does not do is generate a signal of its own. A student can quote this line and lose marks.
fix: A passive sensor (also called externally energised) generates no signal of its own. It converts the measurand into a change of resistance, inductance or capacitance, and an external supply must be present for that change to become a signal.

problem: 'It draws no power to sense' is false: a passive sensor draws power from the excitation supply while it is sensing, and that is exactly why self-heating is a design issue (as the chapter itself says in Section 2 and Worked example 1). The trap's own wording repeats the mistake it warns against.
fix: Calling a passive sensor 'no power needed'. It generates no signal of its own and cannot work without excitation — without the supply the output is zero. Note that it does draw current from that supply, which is why excitation level matters.

problem: 'For a purpose other than measurement' is an added restriction that standard definitions do not carry. Inverse transducers are common inside measurement systems — the pen motor of a chart recorder, the deflection coil of a CRO — so the qualifier can mislead.
fix: An inverse transducer converts an electrical input into a non-electrical output, for example a piezoelectric crystal driven by a voltage to launch ultrasound, or the pen motor that moves the pen of a recorder.

problem: 'emf' is used from the first sentence and never expanded. Many readers will not know it means electromotive force, that is, a source voltage.
fix: Write 'its own emf (electromotive force, a generated voltage)' at first use, then use emf afterwards.

where: Section 2, active list and Worked example 1(b)
problem: '12 mV per g' uses g without definition. In a sensor chapter a reader can take g for gram; it here means the acceleration due to gravity, 9.81 m/s².
fix: '12 mV per g (g = 9.81 m/s², the acceleration due to gravity)' at first use.

problem: 'Digital output travels over long cable without losing accuracy' is too absolute. A digital signal resists noise far better than an analog one, but long cables, ground loops and ringing can still corrupt pulses or code words.
fix: 'Digital output is far more immune to noise over long cable than an analog voltage, though the cable and grounding still have to be done properly.'

problem: 'MEMS' is not expanded anywhere, and the box is meant for reading without other references.
